title.en: The Falcon Called Indi: Manco Capac's Familiar in a Straw Hamper
title.zh: 名喚「因蒂」的鷹:曼科·卡帕克的行囊神鳥

region.en: Road from Tampu-tocco to Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 坦波-托科至庫斯科之路(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Incas and the rest of the ayllus set out from their homes at Tampu-tocco, taking with them their property and arms, having for their chiefs Manco Ccapac and Mama Huaco. Manco Ccapac took with him a bird like a falcon, called indi, which they all worshipped and feared as a sacred, or, as some say, an enchanted thing, for they thought that this bird made Manco Ccapac their lord and obliged the people to follow him. It was carried always in a covered hamper of straw, like a box, with much care. He left it as an heirloom to his son, and the Incas had it down to the time of Inca Yupanqui. In his hand he carried a staff of gold, to test the lands which they would come to.
summary.zh: 印加王族與各阿伊柳世系攜家財兵器,自坦波-托科啟程,以曼科·卡帕克與瑪瑪·瓦科為首領。曼科隨行攜有一隻似隼的鳥,名喚「因蒂」;族人皆奉若神明,敬而且畏——有人說它是受了魔法的靈物,因為人們相信正是這隻鳥使曼科成為他們的主,並驅使民眾追隨於他。此鳥常藏於草編箱籠之中,呵護備至。曼科將它傳給兒子,作為傳家之寶;印加王族一直供奉至印加·尤潘琪之世。他手中另持一根金杖,用以試探將要到來的土地。

sensitivity.note: The dynastic familiar bird; Markham notes the word indi seems identical with Ynti, the Sun.

passages.text: The Incas and the rest of the companies or ayllus set out from their homes at Tampu-tocco, taking with them their property and arms, in sufficient numbers to form a good squadron, having for their chiefs the said Manco Ccapac and Mama Huaco. Manco Ccapac took with him a bird like a falcon, called indi, which they all worshipped and feared as a sacred, or, as some say, an enchanted thing, for they thought that this bird made Manco Ccapac their lord and obliged the people to follow him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was thus that Manco Ccapac gave them to understand, and it was carried always in a covered hamper of straw, like a box, with much care. He left it as an heirloom to his son, and the Incas had it down to the time of Inca Yupanqui. In his hand he carried with him a staff of gold, to test the lands which they would come to.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ayar Cachi Sealed in the Window: The Sling-Hero Betrayed
title.zh: 亞亞爾-卡奇被封於窗內:彈弓英雄之死

region.zh: 坦波-托科「富窗」(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Ayar Cachi was fierce and strong, and very dexterous with the sling: he committed great cruelties and was oppressive both among the natives of the places they passed, and among his own people. The other brothers were afraid that his conduct would cause their companies to disband and desert. Manco Ccapac, being prudent, concurred that they should secure their object by deceit. They called Ayar Cachi: 'Brother! Know that in Ccapac-tocco we have forgotten the golden vases called tupac-cusi, and certain seeds, and the napa, which is our principal ensign of sovereignty' - the napa being a white sheep with a red body cloth, golden ear-rings, and a breast plate with red badges, carried in front of all on a pole with a cross of plumes called suntur-paucar. When Ayar Cachi refused to return, his sister Mama Huaco rebuked him with furious words: 'How is it that there should be such cowardice in so strong a youth as you are? Get ready for the journey.' Shamed, he obeyed; they gave him a companion, Tampu-chacay, with secret orders to kill him at Tampu-tocco. Scarcely had Ayar Cachi entered through the window Ccapac-tocco when Tampu-chacay put a rock against the opening and sat upon it, that Ayar Cachi might remain inside and die there. Ayar Cachi understood the treason, and used such force and shouted so loud that he made the mountain tremble: 'Thou traitor! thou who hast done me so much harm, thinkest thou to convey the news of my mortal imprisonment? That shall never happen. For thy treason thou shalt remain outside, turned into a stone.' So it was done, and to this day they show the stone on one side of the window Ccapac-tocco. The seven brethren were very sorry for what they had done, and mourned for him: Ayar Cachi was so dexterous with a sling and so strong that with each shot he pulled down a mountain and filled up a ravine - the ravines now seen on their line of march were made by Ayar Cachi in hurling stones. From that time to this day the lineage of the Incas always fear to go to Tampu-tocco, lest they should have to remain there like Ayar Cachi.
summary.zh: 亞亞爾-卡奇兇悍有力,彈弓絕技冠絕一時:他對沿途土著與本族同伴橫行暴虐。眾兄弟恐怕他的行徑會使部眾離散。謹慎的曼科·卡帕克與眾人合謀,以欺詐除之。眾人喚他說:「兄弟!我們在卡帕克-托科忘了名為『圖帕克-庫西』的金瓶,還有種子,以及我們至高的王權聖徽『納帕』。」納帕是一頭白羊,披紅衣,戴金耳環,胸前綴紅色徽章,由人擎桿舉於隊首,桿頂插羽十字,稱「孫圖爾-保卡爾」。亞亞爾-卡奇推託不願回去,其姊瑪瑪·瓦科勃然大怒,斥道:「你這般孔武有力的少年,怎會如此怯懦?整裝上路,去吧!」他受辱動身;眾人派同行的坦普-查卡伊隨行,密令他在坦波-托科殺之。二人一到,亞亞爾-卡奇甫入卡帕克-托科之窗,坦普-查卡伊便搬來巨石堵住窗口,坐鎮其上,要把他困死其中。亞亞爾-卡奇識破背叛,奮力撞擊,吼聲震得山嶽發抖:「叛徒!你害我至此,還想報信說我困死於此?永無此事!你這叛徒,就留在窗外,化為石頭吧!」果然應驗——今日人們猶指認富窗一側的那塊石頭。眾兄弟聞其死訊,追悔莫及,為之舉哀:亞亞爾-卡奇彈無虛發,一石下山、一石填谷——如今行軍道上所見的溝壑,便是他當年擲石所成。而印加王族自那時起,始終不敢靠近坦波-托科,生怕自己也像亞亞爾-卡奇那樣被留在窗內。

sensitivity.note: The strongest brother eliminated by trickery - a fratricide at the origin of the dynasty; Garcilaso omits this version entirely.

passages.text: Ayar Cachi was fierce and strong, and very dexterous with the sling. He committed great cruelties and was oppressive both among the natives of the places they passed, and among his own people. The other brothers were afraid that the conduct of Ayar Cachi would cause their companies to disband and desert... As Manco Ccapac was prudent, he concurred with the opinion of the others that they should secure their object by deceit. They called Ayar Cachi and said to him, 'Brother! Know that in Ccapac-tocco we have forgotten the golden vases called tupac-cusi, and certain seeds, and the napa, which is our principal ensign of sovereignty.' The napa is a sheep of the country, the colour white, with a red body cloth, on the top ear-rings of gold, and on the breast a plate with red badges... carried in front of all on a pole with a cross of plumes of feathers. This was called suntur-paucar.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Ayar Cachi refused to return, his sister Mama Huaco, raising her foot, rebuked him with furious words, saying, 'How is it that there should be such cowardice in so strong a youth as you are? Get ready for the journey, and do not fail to go to Tampu-tocco, and do what you are ordered.' Ayar Cachi was shamed by these words. He obeyed and started to carry out his orders. They gave him, as a companion, one of those who had come with them, named Tampu-chacay, to whom they gave secret orders to kill Ayar Cachi at Tampu-tocco, and not to return with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: They had scarcely arrived when Ayar Cachi entered through the window Ccapac-tocco, to get the things for which he had been sent. He was no sooner inside than Tampu-chacay, with great celerity, put a rock against the opening of the window and sat upon it, that Ayar Cachi might remain inside and die there. When Ayar Cachi turned to the opening and found it closed he understood the treason of which the traitor Tampu-chacay had been guilty, and determined to get out if it was possible, to take vengeance. To force an opening he used such force and shouted so loud that he made the mountain tremble. With a loud voice he spoke these words to Tampu-chacay: 'Thou traitor! thou who hast done me so much harm, thinkest thou to convey the news of my mortal imprisonment? That shall never happen. For thy treason thou shalt remain outside, turned into a stone.' So it was done, and to this day they show the stone on one side of the window Ccapac-tocco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The seven brethren who had remained at Hays-quisro were very sorry for what they had done, and mourned for him. This Ayar Cachi was so dexterous with a sling and so strong that with each shot he pulled down a mountain and filled up a ravine. They say that the ravines, which we now see on their line of march, were made by Ayar Cachi in hurling stones. Those of the lineage of the Incas, from that time to this day, always fear to go to Tampu-tocco, lest they should have to remain there like Ayar Cachi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, chs. 12-13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ayar Uchu on the Rainbow Hill: 'Honour Me in All Your Festivals'
title.zh: 彩虹山上的亞亞爾-烏丘:「爾等節慶當尊我」

region.en: Hill of Huanacauri, two leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科兩萊格外瓦納考里山(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Leaving Quirirmanta they came to a hill at a distance of about two leagues from Cuzco. Ascending the hill they saw a rainbow, which the natives call huanacauri. Holding it to be a fortunate sign, Manco Ccapac said: 'Take this for a sign that the world will not be destroyed by water. We shall arrive, and from hence we shall select where we shall found our city.' Before they got to the height where the rainbow was, they saw a huaca which was a place of worship in human shape, near the rainbow. Ayar Uchu offered himself to go to it, for they said that he was very like it. When Ayar Uchu came to the statue or huaca, with great courage he sat upon it, asking it what it did there. At these words the huaca turned its head to see who spoke, but, owing to the weight upon it, it could not see. Presently, when Ayar Uchu wanted to get off he was not able, for he found that the soles of his feet were fastened to the shoulders of the huaca. The six brethren came to succour him, but Ayar Uchu, finding himself transformed and that his brethren could not release him, said to them: 'O Brothers, an evil work you have wrought for me. It was for your sakes that I came where I must remain for ever, apart from your company. Go! go! happy brethren, I announce to you that you will be great lords. I pray that in recognition of the desire I have always had to please you, you will honour and venerate me in all your festivals and ceremonies, and that I shall be the first to whom you make offerings. When you celebrate the huarachico (the arming of the sons as knights) you shall adore me as their father, for I shall remain here for ever.' Manco Ccapac answered that he would do so. Ayar Uchu promised for the youths that he would bestow on them the gifts of valour, nobility, and knighthood, and with these last words he remained, turned into stone. They constituted him the huaca of the Incas, giving it the name of Ayar Uchu Huanacauri; and so it always was, until the arrival of the Spaniards, the most venerated huaca, and the one that received the most offerings of any in the kingdom.
summary.zh: 離開基里爾曼塔,他們來到庫斯科約兩萊格外的一座山。登山之際,望見一道彩虹,土人稱之「瓦納考里」。曼科·卡帕克視為吉兆,說道:「以此為記——世界將不再毀於洪水。我們就要在此擇地建城。」未到彩虹之巔,他們先見一座人形瓦卡——崇拜之所——立於彩虹近旁。因說亞亞爾-烏丘與它極為相似,他自告奮勇前往。他大膽坐上神像,喝問它在此做什麼。瓦卡聞聲轉頭想看清來人,卻因身上負重而不能;待亞亞爾-烏丘起身離開,卻發現自己的腳掌已黏連在瓦卡的肩上,再也動彈不得。六位兄弟上前施救,無濟於事。亞亞爾-烏丘見自己已然變形,對兄弟們說:「兄弟們啊,你們害苦了我。為了你們,我來到此地,從此永離你們的行列。去吧!去吧!快樂的兄弟們,我預告你們:你們必成大主。求你們念我一貫討你們歡心的心願,在一切節慶祭典中尊崇我、敬奉我,讓我受祭於最先。我永留於此。你們為兒子們行瓦拉奇庫受武禮時,當以父禮拜我——因為我永在。」曼科·卡帕克應允。亞亞爾-烏丘代少年們承諾:他將賜他們勇武、高貴與騎士之名。言畢,他化為頑石。眾人立他為印加人的瓦卡,名之「亞亞爾-烏丘·瓦納考里」。直到西班牙人到來之前,它始終是王國中最受尊崇、受祭最豐的瓦卡。

sensitivity.note: The origin of the principal huaca of Cuzco from a petrified brother; the rainbow omen ties to the post-flood promise.

title.en: The Golden Wand in the Furrow: Testing the Soil of Huanay-pata
title.zh: 金杖插犁溝:試探瓦納伊-帕塔之土

region.zh: 庫斯科附近瓦納伊-帕塔(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: They were in Matahua for two years, waiting to pass on to the upper valley to seek good and fertile land. Mama Huaco, who was very strong and dexterous, took two wands of gold and hurled them towards the north. One fell, at two shots of an arquebus distance, into a ploughed field called Colcapampa and did not drive in well, the soil being loose and not terraced: by this they knew that the soil was not fertile. The other went further, to near Cuzco, and fixed well in the territory called Huanay-pata, where they knew the land to be fertile. Others say that this proof was made by Manco Ccapac with the staff of gold which he carried himself, and that thus they knew of the fertility of the land, when the staff sunk in the land called Huanay-pata, two shots of an arquebus from Cuzco. They knew the crust of the soil to be rich and close, so that it could only be broken by using much force. Let it be by one way or the other, for all agree that they went trying the land with a pole or staff until they arrived at this Huanay-pata, when they were satisfied: they were sure of its fertility, because after sowing perpetually, it always yielded abundantly, giving more the more it was sown.
summary.zh: 眾人在馬塔瓦駐留兩年,等待進入上谷另覓沃土。瑪瑪·瓦孔武而靈巧,取兩支金杖向北方擲去。一支落在兩火槍射程之外、名為科爾卡潘帕的犁田之中,插入不深——土壤鬆散、未經築台——眾人知此地不肥。另一支飛得更遠,近庫斯科處,穩穩插入名為瓦納伊-帕塔的土地——眾人知此地肥沃。另一說:此試乃曼科·卡帕克親持金杖所為;金杖深插瓦納伊-帕塔之土,便知此地肥美:表土豐厚緊實,非大力不能破土。無論何說,眾人皆沿途以杖試土,直至瓦納伊-帕塔方才滿意:此地耕之不輟,歲歲豐登,愈種愈多。

sensitivity.note: The gold-staff divination of the founding; the female thrower variant credits Mama Huaco.

title.en: Ayar Auca Takes Flight: The Stone of Possession and the Name of Cuzco
title.zh: 亞亞爾-奧卡飛臨:鎮地之石與「庫斯科」之名

region.en: Site of Santo Domingo, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科聖多明我修道院舊址(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: From that place Manco Ccapac saw a heap of stones near the site of the present monastery of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Pointing it out to his brother Ayar Auca, he said: 'Brother! you remember how it was arranged between us, that you should go to take possession of the land where we are to settle. Well! look at that stone. Go thither flying' - for they say that Ayar Auca had developed some wings - 'and seating yourself there, take possession of land seen from that heap of stones. We will presently come to settle and reside.' When Ayar Auca heard the words of his brother, he opened his wings and flew to that place which Manco Ccapac had pointed out. Seating himself there, he was presently turned into stone, and was made the stone of possession. In the ancient language of this valley the heap was called cozco, whence that site has had the name of Cuzco to this day. From this circumstance the Incas had a proverb which said: 'Ayar Auca cuzco huanca' - Ayar Auca a heap of marble. Others say that Manco Ccapac gave the name of Cuzco because he wept in that place where he buried his brother Ayar Cachi; owing to his sorrow and to the fertility he gave that name which in the ancient language of that time signified sad as well as fertile.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克在馬塔瓦遙指庫斯科今聖多明我修道院附近的一堆亂石,對兄弟亞亞爾-奧卡說:「兄弟!你記得我們的約定——由你去佔領我們將定居的土地。看那石頭!飛過去吧」——相傳亞亞爾-奧卡此時生出了翅膀——「落在那裡,以那堆石所見之地為你所有。我們隨後就來定居。」亞亞爾-奧卡聞言展翼,飛至曼科所指之處,一坐之下,頓時化作石頭——是為「鎮地之石」。在谷地的古語中,那堆石頭稱「科茲科」,此地因此得名庫斯科,沿稱至今。印加王族由此留下一句諺語:「亞亞爾-奧卡,庫斯科-萬卡」——亞亞爾-奧卡,一堆大理石。另有異說:庫斯科之名,是曼科·卡帕克葬其弟亞亞爾-卡奇於此,因哀傷與此地之肥沃而命名——古語中此名兼有「悲傷」與「肥沃」二義。前一說更可信,因亞亞爾-卡奇實死於卡帕克-托科,並未葬於庫斯科;印加人與土人皆如此公認。

sensitivity.note: The winged brother as founding stone; Sarmiento weighs two rival etymologies of Cuzco and prefers the stone-of-possession version.

passages.text: From that place Manco Ccapac saw a heap of stones near the site of the present monastery of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Pointing it out to his brother Ayar Auca, he said, 'Brother! you remember how it was arranged between us, that you should go to take possession of the land where we are to settle. Well! look at that stone. Go thither flying' - for they say that Ayar Auca had developed some wings - 'and seating yourself there, take possession of land seen from that heap of stones. We will presently come to settle and reside.' When Ayar Auca heard the words of his brother, he opened his wings and flew to that place which Manco Ccapac had pointed out. Seating himself there, he was presently turned into stone, and was made the stone of possession.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the ancient language of this valley the heap was called cozco, whence that site has had the name of Cuzco to this day. From this circumstance the Incas had a proverb which said, 'Ayar Auca cuzco huanca,' or, 'Ayar Auca a heap of marble.' Others say that Manco Ccapac gave the name of Cuzco because he wept in that place where he buried his brother Ayar Cachi. Owing to his sorrow and to the fertility he gave that name which in the ancient language of that time signified sad as well as fertile.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Heart in Her Mouth: Mama Occlo Terrorizes the Huallas
title.zh: 口銜心肺:瑪瑪·奧克略懾服瓜利亞斯人

region.zh: 庫斯科附近瓦納伊-帕塔(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Arriving on the land of Huanay-pata, Manco Ccapac found settled there a nation of Indians named Huallas. Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo began to settle and to take possession of the land and water, against the will of the Huallas; in this business they did many violent and unjust things. As the Huallas attempted to defend their lives and properties, many cruelties were committed. They relate that Mama Occlo was so fierce that, having killed one of the Hualla Indians, she cut him up, took out the inside, carried the heart and lungs in her mouth, and with an ayuinto, which is a stone fastened to a rope, in her hand, she attacked the Huallas with diabolical resolution. When the Huallas beheld this horrible and inhuman spectacle, they feared that the same thing would be done to them, being simple and timid, and they fled and abandoned their rights. Mama Occlo, reflecting on her cruelty, and fearing that for it they would be branded as tyrants, resolved not to spare any Huallas, believing that the affair would thus be forgotten. So they killed all they could lay their hands upon, dragging infants from their mothers' wombs, that no memory might be left of these miserable Huallas.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克進抵瓦納伊-帕塔,該處已定居著瓜利亞斯族。曼科與瑪瑪·奧克略不顧瓜利亞斯人意願,強行佔田奪水,行事兇暴不義。瓜利亞斯人自衛保命,遂遭種種殘害。相傳瑪瑪·奧克略兇悍至極:殺了一名瓜利亞斯人後,碎其屍,掏出內臟,竟將心肺銜於口中,手持繫繩的拋石「亞溫托」,以惡魔般的狠勁向瓜利亞斯人衝殺。瓜利亞斯人見此慘狀,自忖弱小怯懦,恐怕自己也要遭此毒手,遂棄地而逃,放棄了一切權利。瑪瑪·奧克略自忖殘忍太過,恐被人斥為暴君,便決計斬盡殺絕,以為如此便可抹去罪跡。於是凡力所能及者盡數殺戮,甚至從母腹中拖出嬰兒,務使這些可憐的瓜利亞斯人無人記憶。

sensitivity.note: Sarmiento's indictment of the founding violence - he wrote to prove Inca 'tyranny' for Viceroy Toledo; the atrocity story is quoted as the sworn testimony he recorded.

As the Huallas attempted to defend their lives and properties, many cruelties were committed by Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo.

When the Huallas beheld this horrible and inhuman spectacle, they feared that the same thing would be done to them, being simple and timid, and they fled and abandoned their rights.

title.en: Copalimayta Stands: The Sinchi Who Was Erased
title.zh: 科帕利馬伊塔的抗爭:被抹去的辛奇

region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Having done this Manco Ccapac advanced, and came within a mile of Cuzco to the S.E., where a Sinchi named Copalimayta came out to oppose him - a late-comer who had settled with the consent of the natives of the valley, incorporated in the nation of Sauaseray Panaca, natives of the site of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Having seen the strangers invading their lands and tyrannizing over them, and knowing the cruelties inflicted on the Huallas, they had chosen Copalimayta as their Sinchi. He came forth to resist the invasion, saying that the strangers should not enter his lands or those of the natives. His resistance was such that Manco Ccapac and his companions were obliged to turn their backs. They returned to Huanay-pata, the land they had usurped from the Huallas; from the sowing they had made they derived a fine crop of maize, and for this reason they gave the place a name which means something precious. After some months they returned to the attack on the natives of the valley: they assaulted the settlement of the Sauaseras and captured Copalimayta, slaughtering many of the Sauaseras with great cruelty. Copalimayta, finding himself a prisoner and fearing death, fled out of desperation, leaving his estates, and was never seen again after he escaped. Mama Huaco and Manco Ccapac usurped his houses, lands and people. In this way Manco Ccapac, Mama Huaco, Sinchi Rocca and Manco Sapaca settled on the site between the two rivers, and erected the House of the Sun, which they called Ynti-cancha. They divided that position into four neighbourhoods or quarters, which they call cancha: Quinti-cancha, Chumpi-cancha, Sayri-cancha and Yarampuy-cancha.
summary.zh: 行此之後,曼科·卡帕克推進至庫斯科東南約一哩處,辛奇科帕利馬伊塔出而拒之。此人雖屬後來者,但經谷地土著同意入居,併入聖多明我舊址的薩瓦塞雷·帕納卡族。他們見外來者侵田凌民,又聞瓜利亞斯人慘遭荼毒,便推科帕利馬伊塔為辛奇。他起而抗侵入,聲言:「外人不得踏入我的土地、土著的土地!」其抵抗之烈,竟使曼科·卡帕克一夥敗退。他們退回從瓜利亞斯人手中奪來的瓦納伊-帕塔;所播玉米大豐,遂以「珍寶」之意為此地命名。數月後,他們捲土重來,再攻谷中土著:夜襲薩瓦塞拉斯聚落,俘科帕利馬伊塔,殘殺眾多族人。科帕利馬伊塔淪為囚徒,懼死而拼死出逃,棄其田宅,自此杳無音訊。瑪瑪·瓦科與曼科·卡帕克遂奪其屋、其田、其民。曼科·卡帕克、瑪瑪·瓦科、辛奇·羅卡與曼科·薩帕卡自此定居兩河之間,興建太陽之屋「因蒂-坎恰」;又將這片地方劃為四坊(坎恰):金蒂、瓊皮、賽里、亞蘭普伊。

sensitivity.note: The erased resister; Sarmiento's record is unusual in preserving the names of the dispossessed.

Having seen the strangers invading their lands and tyrannizing over them, and knowing the cruelties inflicted on the Huallas, they had chosen Copalimayta as their Sinchi. He came forth to resist the invasion, saying that the strangers should not enter his lands or those of the natives. His resistance was such that Manco Ccapac and his companions were obliged to turn their backs.

passages.text: After some months they returned to the attack on the natives of the valley, to tyrannize over them. They assaulted the settlement of the Sauaseras, and were so rapid in their attack that they captured Copalimayta, slaughtering many of the Sauaseras with great cruelty. Copalimayta, finding himself a prisoner and fearing death, fled out of desperation, leaving his estates, and was never seen again after he escaped. Mama Huaco and Manco Ccapac usurped his houses, lands and people.

They divided all that position, from Santo Domingo to the junction of the rivers into four neighbourhoods or quarters which they call cancha. They called one Quinti-cancha, the second Chumpi-cancha, the third Sayri-cancha, and the fourth Yarampuy-cancha.
